body:
## Summary
The Claude Code OTLP push path stores delta counters by INCREMENTING day buckets and session rows, and nothing records which datapoints were already admitted. OTLP delivery is at-least-once: a timeout, a 502/504 from the platform after the write committed, or a mid-batch DB failure makes the exporter resend the same export, and every resend adds the same dollars again. Measured spend is the one tier Ascent calls exact (providers.ts:7); it is also the only tier with no replay defence. This card makes admission idempotent at the store, per datapoint, per sink.

## Description
Applies usage-event-ingestion (golden path, 'De-duplication is the emitter's promise, enforced by your store') together with its running-total-or-increment technique, which this path already honours for temporality. OTLP carries no transmission id, so the key is the closest emitter-minted identity: series identity (source, metric name, sorted resource attributes, sorted datapoint attributes) plus the delta interval (startTimeUnixNano, timeUnixNano). A delta series cannot legitimately report the same interval twice, so this is identity, not a content hash of values: two genuine increments of equal value in different intervals never collide (acceptance 3). Record this as a deviation note in the doc: the standard prefers an emitter-chosen transmission key, OTLP does not offer one, and interval identity is the substitute.

Uniqueness lives in the store: a new OtlpPointReceipt(orgId, sink, pointKey, createdAt) with @@unique([orgId, sink, pointKey]). Admission is one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING pointKey inside an interactive transaction; only returned keys are folded, and the bucket/session writes run in the SAME transaction so a failure rolls back the claim with the write (acceptance 5). Two sinks (usage, sessions) claim independently, preserving the route's existing rule that a session-write failure never fails an ingest whose usage landed (route.ts:66-69). A duplicate is terminal: 202 with duplicates:n, never a retriable status. Receipts expire after a 7-day replay horizon, swept for the ingesting org in-request with a bounded delete, so no retention.ts change is needed.

## Flow
- otlp-wire.ts: read startTimeUnixNano.
- otlp-point-key.ts (pure): pointKey(source, resourceAttrs, metricName, dp) -> sha256 hex, or null when the datapoint has no time at all (admitted as unkeyed).
- otlp.ts / sessions.ts: accept an optional admit(key) predicate so parse stays pure and testable; parseOtlpMetrics also returns the keys it would consume.
- otlp-receipts.ts: claimPoints(tx, orgId, sink, keys) -> Set of new keys; sweepExpired(tx, orgId).
- integrations.ts / agent-sessions.ts: optional db client param (default getPrisma()) so they run inside the tx; signatures otherwise unchanged.
- metrics route: claim -> parse(admit) -> write, per sink, in prisma.$transaction; response gains duplicates and unkeyed.

## Expected impact
Measured per-repo spend, AgentSession cost-per-attempt and every Delivery ROI figure built on them stop drifting upward with network weather. Today an inflated number is indistinguishable from real usage: nothing in the store can tell them apart after the fact.

## Evaluation
Claim: a replayed or partially-failed OTLP export is stored exactly once.
Before: 0 of 8 cases pass (1, 2, 4, 5 double-count; 6-8 have no mechanism to test)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first (route.replay.test.ts against the PGlite-backed test db; otlp-point-key.test.ts pure)
Result: better
Gate: contract (new table + migration; ingest response gains fields, nothing removed)

body:
## Summary
An owner connects Claude Code, the Integrations card turns green with '3 repos attributed', and the AI delivery view shows no spend for two of them, because Delivery only draws repos that have scanned PR signals and silently ignores measured usage on any other repo. The decision 'is my spend actually reaching the ROI view?' is made blind even though both sides of the join are already in the database. This card shows the reconciliation and lets the owner fix it in one move.

## Description
A server read (integrations-attribution.ts) returns the org's measured scope=repo usage per repo over the Delivery window, joined against the SAME set Delivery joins against (getOrgPrSignals.perRepo, lower-cased) plus Repository existence. One authority for the join, so the reconcile cannot disagree with Delivery. A pure attributionReconcileModel buckets each repo as landed / inFleetNoSignals / outsideFleet, computes hidden spend and its share, and builds the scan plan. AttributionReconcile renders it under the Claude Code connect surface in both compositions (Prism ClaudeConnect.v2, Altimeter IntegrationsTab.v1): '$10.00 of $50.00 measured spend (20%) lands on 1 repository AI delivery cannot show', the repos with their cost, and one 'Scan 1 repository' button whose count is disclosed before it runs. The action uses runImportScan with watch:false/schedule:'off', so it is a one-shot scan the owner chose, never a silent recurring subscription; the import route keeps every gate and credit rule it has. The connection ladder stops calling an invisible attribution 'reached'.

Registry: adoption-measurement / attribution-provenance-tiers (a number displayed must carry what it is counted over) and the 'unknown is not a value' law for the no-rows state.

## Flow
- IntegrationsTab (owner-gated) -> getMeasuredAttribution(slug) -> IntegrationsData.attribution (wire-safe: ISO strings, cents).
- reconcile(attribution) -> buckets + hiddenCostCents + scanPlan.
- AttributionReconcile: list + disclosed button -> useAttributionScan -> runImportScan -> per-repo progress -> router.refresh() so the buckets re-derive.
- integrationLadder: claude 'On a repository' becomes reached only when at least one measured repo is landed.

## Expected impact
The gap between 'telemetry arrived' and 'ROI shows it' becomes a named, actionable number on the page where the owner connects the provider, and closing it is one click instead of discovering it on another tab, finding the repo names, and importing them by hand.

## Evaluation
Claim: the owner sees which measured spend Delivery cannot show and can scan those repos in one action.
Before: 0 of 7 cases pass (no per-repo read, no model, the ladder reads reached)
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first against attributionReconcileModel (pure), integrationLadder, and integrations-attribution (test db)
Result: better
Gate: none

The economics-1 fix (groupBy latest-per-repo, then fetch only those rows) landed in three readers and was explicitly written 'so the call sites cannot drift'. Ten sibling fleet readers still use the nested `scans: { take: N }` shape the module's own header measures as transferring the org's whole scan history, and two of them (practices, gap analysis) still fold mock-floor scans that getOrgRollup refuses. Make `org-rollup-latest-scans.ts` the only door to 'the latest scan per repo', add a real-only option the dimension aggregators use, and pin it with a source-scanning guard.

## Description
Applies metrics-rollups / cardinality-and-cost ('bounding a grouped read before it ships') and measurement-honesty / co-published-numbers-must-reconcile: the Practices tab, gap analysis and the rollup badge sit on the same pages and must count the same population. The guard follows AGENTS.md's rule for source-scanning gates: strip comments and string literals before matching, and seed a violation that must keep failing.

- Add `readLatestTwoScansPerRepo` (groupBy + scanAtBeforePerRepo + atPairs) beside readLatestScanPerRepo.
- Migrate getOrgRecommendations, getOrgPractices, getOrgGapAnalysis, getOrgDiscrepancies (insights); getOrgPrSignals, getOrgGovernance, getOrgDimensionGaps, getOrgActivity (signals); getOrgTeamRollup (teams); getRepoStates, getOrgHeaderSummary (rollup).

## Expected impact
Every org page header (cache()d summary) and every Standing/Shared/Bought tab stops reading O(fleet x age) Scan rows; the Practice Library and gap analysis stop reporting mock placeholders as org gaps beside a badge that excludes them.

## Summary
When a period is selected, every scoped tab prints the same fixed caveat that some repos are in the average but not in movers. The user cannot tell whether that is 0 repos or 30, which ones, or how stale they are, and has to go to Repositories, filter by last-scan date and rescan by hand. The rollup on the page already knows the answer. Turn the caveat into a counted, named strip with one action: rescan the carried repos.

## Description
A pure `periodCoverageModel.ts` derives, from the rollup rows and window.start: in-period vs carried counts, the carried repos oldest-first, which are already queued for a rescore, which are unwatched (the bulk route cannot scan them), and the rescan set. `PeriodCoverageStrip` renders it beside the fleet numbers on Overview and Teams; `PeriodCoverageRescan` hands the set to the existing `useOrgScanButton().run({ repos })`, so credits, auth and the durable queue all stay exactly as they are. ScopeFilterBar's caption becomes counted when coverage is supplied and keeps the static sentence otherwise. Applies metrics-rollups / aggregate-honesty ('count-carries-predicate'): the average says which population it stands on.

## Flow
- Overview / Teams compute coverage from the rollup they already awaited.
- Strip: '7 of 42 repos have no scan this period (oldest: api, 41 days)' + expandable list + 'Rescan 4' (2 already queued, 1 not watched).
- Click -> named-repo bulk scan through the existing stream + queue follow; router refresh on settle.

## Expected impact
A blind disclaimer becomes a decision with its data and its fix on the same surface: five steps (notice, go to Repositories, sort, select, rescan) become one, and the 'is this a bug?' question the caption exists to answer is answered with numbers.

## Evaluation
Claim: the period split is counted, named and actionable
Before: 0 of 6 cases pass (static caption case green by design)
After: 6 of 6
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: none

body:
## Summary
The report states one dimension's share of the headline in three places and two derivations. The waterfall divides by the sum of PRESENT weights (contributions()); the Dimensions explorer, its reading strip and the detail headline multiply by the raw lens weight. On every full scan the lenses sum to 1.00 and nobody notices; on a dropped-dimension scan (D9 unmeasured, a failed detector) the Dimensions tab understates every 'in reach' lever by ~10% and prints 'weight 15%' where the Scoring tab prints 'x 16%' for the same dimension. The level-band edges are the same fork: chartScale hand-types 85/65/45/25 and three sites type the L4 floor 65, while AltimeterGauge already derives its strata from LEVELS.

## Description
Apply data-viz/metric-identity 'one derivation, many surfaces' and 'forced duplication gets a parity gate': export one share derivation from projections.ts (contributions() becomes its first caller), have dimFacts take the share instead of re-multiplying, render the weight% from it in DimensionReading and DimensionDetail, and derive LEVEL_BANDS / BAND_EDGES / the L4 reference from LEVELS. A parity test runs the explorer and the waterfall over shared fixtures (full, dropped, single, all-zero, other lens) so the next change to either side fails loudly.

## Flow
- projections.ts: `dimensionShares(dims)` -> Map<id, normalizedWeight>; contributions() uses it
- dimensionExplorerDerive.ts: dimFacts(d, prev, integrity, share); DimensionExplorer computes shares once
- DimensionReading / DimensionDetail: print Math.round(share*100)
- chartScale.ts: LEVEL_BANDS mins + BAND_EDGES + L4 floor from LEVELS; Sparkline, DimLine, explorerSummary read it
- dimensionShareParity.test.ts: shared fixtures, tolerance 1e-9

## Expected impact
The two tabs that answer 'where should I invest' stop disagreeing on the lever size on exactly the degraded scans where the reader most needs it; a rubric band retune moves every chart instead of only the Altimeter and the colors.

## Evaluation
Claim: one share derivation and one band source; parity is gated
Before: 0 of 7 cases pass
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: architecture

## Summary
The Scoring tab tells a reader the score moved ('+4 since last scan') and then explains only where the score IS. The waterfall already decomposes the headline into weight x score points; the report already holds the baseline scan and its per-dimension scores. Nobody joins them, so 'why did we gain four points?' is answered by opening /report/compare and doing weighted arithmetic in your head, because the compare page reports raw score deltas, not points.

## Description
Add a 'Since last scan' mode to the ScoreWaterfall: a bridge from the previous overall to this one, one signed step per dimension that moved (share x score delta), entered/left steps for dimensions present on one side only, and one explicit 'rounding & reweighting' residual so the bridge sums exactly to the DeltaPill. Mixed engines and a rubric change are stated above the steps with the existing caveat vocabulary - labelled, never hidden. The pure model (scoreBridgeModel.ts) owns all arithmetic; the surface only presents. Applies data-viz/metric-identity (one derivation: shares from contributions(), never re-multiplied) and the waterfall's own identity (parts sum to the headline).

## Flow
- computeReportSeries exposes the baseline it already picks (additive)
- ReportView -> ReportPanels -> ScoringTab -> ScoreWaterfall(baseline)
- Toggle appears only when the baseline carries dimensions
- Since last scan: '58 -> 62 (+4)', steps biggest |pts| first, residual last, caveats on top

## Expected impact
The most-asked question after any re-scan (what moved my number) is answered on the tab that shows the number, in the unit the number is in, with no navigation and no new fetch.

## Evaluation
Claim: the delta pill becomes attributable in place

After: 7 of 7

## Summary
The price of one model call is decided in three places that disagree: the env-rate estimator (scan lane headline), the built-in table fold (scan per-team/per-repo/matrix cells and the scan unpriced count) and the meter's costMicrosFor (every ledger lane). Move the rule into one module, `src/lib/db/usage-pricing.ts`, that takes (provider, model, byom, tokens) and a resolved basis and returns {usd|null, reason: priced|zero-cost|byom|no-usage|unknown-model}; every fold and the meter call it.

## Description
Registry: cost-metering / price-tables ('one table, one authority ... every consumer imports it'). Today with LLM_*_COST_PER_MTOK set: (1) the scan lane prices GPU-local tokens at the operator's hosted rate while the table path prices them $0; (2) env-priced unknown-model scans are still counted 'unpriced', so the headline wrongly reads as a floor; (3) Spend-by-team, Top repositories and the showback matrix price the scan half from the table while the lane row uses env, so the 'reconcile by construction' claim fails. Separately, the ledger counts zero-cost calls as unpriced while the scan lane counts them priced, and the team panel shows a partial sum with no floor. The basis is resolved ONCE per summary and passed to every fold; teamTotals gains the per-field _count trick repoTotals already uses.

## Flow
- new usage-pricing.ts: resolveScanBasis(env) + priceCallGroup(group, basis) + the reason enum
- usage.ts: scan lane, scanRepoUsage, scanTeamUsage and unpricedScanCalls all fold through priceCallGroup with the one basis; old exports re-exported
- meter.ts: costMicrosFor delegates (zero-cost -> 0 micros, reason zero-cost); an explicit caller costMicros:null is still honoured, so lane-cost.ts's local half is unchanged
- usage-events.ts: TeamUsage.unpricedCalls; mergeTeamUsage sums it; usageLanePanels prints the floor

## Expected impact
Every dollar on /usage and in both showback CSVs is produced by one rule; headline, lane, team, repo and matrix reconcile under any basis. No credit, price, quota or charge changes: estimate display only.

## Evaluation
Claim: one pricing rule makes every /usage fold agree under env rates and local providers

After: 6 of 6

Result: better

## Summary
/usage tells an operator '$211.51 · floor: +45 calls unpriced' and 'Team @acme/web · $40' and stops. Every figure becomes a door: clicking a repo row, a matrix cell or the floor opens a calls panel on the same page and window - the underlying UsageEvent rows, most expensive first, failed calls separated, and every unpriced call tagged with its one reason (BYOM / zero-cost / no usage / unknown model) and whether a rate would ever close it.

## Description
Registry: cost-metering / spend-observability ('Outlier calls, individually ... a most-expensive-calls view'; 'failed-call spend ... broken down by failure reason'). The ledger already carries everything (provider, model, byom, tokens, costMicros, status, team, repo), and an audit read was written for exactly this and never wired to any surface. The decision the operator makes blind today: is the floor something a configured rate fixes, or closed by design? The app has the per-row data to answer it. Scan-lane rows are out of scope for the row list (Scan is its own ledger); the panel says so.

## Flow
- click '45 unpriced' / a repo row / a matrix cell -> /usage?org&days&calls=<filter> (server-rendered, no client JS)
- page parses the filter with usageCallsModel.parseCallsFilter; a bad filter renders no panel
- usage-ledger-read.listLedgerCalls reads the filtered rows over the SAME UsageWindow the page resolves once (page.tsx:90)
- usageCallsPanel renders the reason summary + top 50 rows (priced desc, failed group, unpriced with reason + fix line only where a fix exists)
- view=calls JSON on /api/usage for scripting, same gate

## Expected impact
Turns three report-only spend panels into an investigable ledger; the floor stops being a shrug. No change to what is metered, priced or charged.

## Evaluation

## Summary
The active org is written by one rule and read by another. POST /api/org/active was repaired to validate with canReadOrg, the gate the live Supabase stack enforces. getActiveOrg, which every reader uses, still validates against the dormant custom-OAuth session, and that session is never minted in production. So a remembered org cannot be read back, bare /org always lands on /org/public, /usage defaults to public, and the header shows no switcher at all under the wall. Lift the rule into one resolver that both stacks feed and every reader consults.

## Description
Applies authorization/read-write-predicate-symmetry (laws one-validation-door, one-authority-per-vocabulary): a visibility rule enforced on one path must be enforced on the other in the same terms. Today they disagree in the dangerous direction for UX (the read is stricter than the write, so the choice silently resets) and the code has two vocabularies for 'orgs this viewer may select': dormant installations versus memberships.

A pure `viewer-workspace-model.ts` takes `{ dormantSession, memberships, cookieOrg }` and returns `{ options, active }`: options are dormant installations unioned with memberships (case-insensitive dedupe, original casing kept), then 'public' last. The active org is the cookie if it is an option, else the primary membership or first installation, else 'public'. A thin loader `viewer-workspace.ts` reads getSession(), getViewer()/resolveViewerLogin(), listOrgsForLogin() and the cookie, all in the render/route body (never inside a ReadableStream start(), where cookie reads return null). Brand.tsx's Supabase branch renders OrgSwitcher from it, and /org and /usage use its `active`. auth.ts is not edited: getActiveOrg stays for any dormant-only caller, with no call sites left in the app.

No authorization moves. The cookie only picks a default tenant, every destination still runs its own gate (org layout, requireOrgRead), and the option set is proven to be a subset of canReadOrg by a property test. selfHosted() is not involved.

## Flow
- viewer-workspace-model.ts: resolveWorkspace() pure, unit-tested red-first (cases 1-4)
- viewer-workspace.ts: resolveViewerWorkspace() loader with injected deps, dbReadSafe fallback (cases 7-8)
- Brand.tsx HeaderAccount: Supabase branch renders <OrgSwitcher> when options.length > 1 (case 5)
- org/page.tsx and usage/page.tsx: swap getActiveOrg(session) for (await resolveViewerWorkspace()).active (case 6)
- docs: auth.md function table gains the resolver, org-intelligence.md notes the switcher is live under the wall

## Expected impact
The header org switcher exists in production for every member of two or more orgs. A chosen org survives navigation and revisits. /org and /usage open on the viewer's real tenant instead of the public funnel. The next reader of 'which org is this viewer in?' has one function to call, not a dormant-stack trap.

## Evaluation
Claim: under the Supabase wall the active org written by POST /api/org/active is read back, and the switcher renders
Before: 0 of 8 cases pass (cases 3 and 4 are guards, green-before by design; 6 red)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: architecture - one resolver replaces three call sites; no auth predicate changes

## Summary
A production user who signs in and lands on /onboarding sees a cold start. The page reads installations, discovered org suggestions and the seeded org from the dormant custom-OAuth cookie, which the live Supabase stack never mints. All three wizard shortcuts (installation picker, 'you might want to scan...' suggestions, seeded-org banner) and the 'Welcome back' jump are therefore dead, and so is 'Sign out everywhere else', even though its route already works on the live stack. The sign-in callback computes the ranked org suggestions in after() and then throws them away. Persist what sign-in already learned, read installations through the dual-stack resolver, and render the session controls that work on the live stack.

## Description
The user decides which org to scan blind while the app holds the answer. Applies wizard-flows/snapshot-and-resume ("resume re-runs expensive work already done": keep the discovery result instead of discarding it) and wizard-flows/progress-communication (the step should reflect what the flow already knows: an installed App should not read as 'not installed').

1. Store: a standalone `LoginDiscovery { login @id (lowercased), suggestedOrgs String[], seededOrg String?, discoveredAt }` beside SessionRevocation, plus `src/lib/db/login-discovery.ts` with recordLoginDiscovery / getLoginDiscovery (dbReadSafe, null when the DB is off).
2. Producer: the Supabase callback's existing after() task awaits discoverOrgsForLogin and records the result keyed on the identity Supabase just returned from exchangeCodeForSession (user_metadata.user_name). It never uses a request parameter. A failed discovery ({}) does not overwrite.
3. Reader: `src/lib/onboarding-context.ts` resolveOnboardingContext(deps) picks the dormant session when one exists (unchanged). Otherwise it uses viewerInstallations() plus getLoginDiscovery(viewer.login), drops already-installed orgs from the suggestions, and names which session controls apply ('dormant' | 'supabase' | null). It is awaited in the page body, never inside a stream start().
4. Surface: onboarding/page.tsx feeds OnboardingFlow and the Welcome-back candidates from the context. SessionControls takes a `stack` prop: under the wall it renders the working revoke form and hides the resync buttons, which cannot complete there.

Auth is untouched. Discovery is read only for the resolved viewer's own login, installations come from memberships, and the repo load is still gated by requireOrgRead. The stored data is the viewer's own public org memberships, which the session cookie used to carry.

## Flow
- schema + migration: LoginDiscovery table
- db/login-discovery.ts: record/get, unit-tested (case 8)
- auth/callback/route.ts after(): discover then record (cases 1-2)
- onboarding-context.ts: pure-ish resolver with injected deps (cases 3-6)
- onboarding/page.tsx: consume context; SessionControls stack prop (case 7)
- docs: delete the two Known gaps in auth.md, update wizard.md shortcuts and data-model.md table list

## Expected impact
On the stack that is production, the first screen after sign-in offers the user's installed orgs as one-click sources and the orgs they are most active in as suggestions. The seeded org's ready dashboard is pointed at, a returning user gets the Welcome-back jump, and 'Sign out everywhere else' is reachable. Today a production user can reach none of these.

## Evaluation

After: 8 of 8

## Summary
The claim path decides who wins a row with a compare-and-set, but every write after the claim checks only the holder's name. A token whose lease lapsed and was re-claimed by its own second session can still report on the new claim. Mint a fence at claim time, require it on every later write, and drop the name-keyed holder arm that should have gone in September.

## Description
`reportAttempt` and `heldFollowups` authorize on `claimActor IN (actor, legacyActor)` plus `status = in_progress` (followup-claims.ts:374, :398). The registry technique this module was forged from (remediation-handoff / handoff-tenancy-and-idempotence) names that exact case as the defect: a paused worker does not know its lease lapsed, and the same identity claiming again looks just like the stale holder. `npx ascent work run` makes the window ordinary, because it claims, runs an agent of any length, then reports every id (ascent-work.mjs:172-193).

The fence costs no schema change. `leaseUntil` is already unique per claim, round-trips at millisecond precision, and is carried across rescans by `claimCarry`. The technique itself says 'the lease value itself will do'. A leased claim's fence is its lease, and an unleased claim (human, local lane) has a null fence, which keeps the 'null is never expired' rule.

Two debts go with it, because both are generation questions:
- the transitional `legacyActor` arm (followup-claims.ts:322-336), still populated at the door (mcp/route.ts:278) 47 days after its 'within a day' end date;
- `needsHuman`, which no write ever clears (followup-claims.ts:238 and :383), so a reopened row carries a stale escalation into its next claim.

## Flow
- Add pure `fenceOf(leaseUntil)` and `fenceVerdict(stored, presented) -> ok | stale | unfenced` in followups-claims.ts, with a red-first unit test.
- Move reportAttempt, heldFollowups and the holder clause into followup-attempts.ts, re-exported from followup-claims.ts. The CAS WHERE gains `leaseUntil = fence` when the row is leased, and the result becomes discriminated: ok, not-held, stale-claim or unfenced.
- claimFollowups returns `fence` on each row, and its data resets `needsHuman: false`.
- MCP: report_attempt's schema gains `fence`, the tool maps stale-claim and unfenced to their own refusal text, and claim/brief return the fence. Remove `legacyActor` from McpPrincipal and the route.
- ascent-work.mjs keeps an id -> fence map from the claim and passes it on every report.
- Doc: the README's claim section gains the fence rule.

## Expected impact
A superseded session can no longer write an attempt, a needs-human flag or a skipped release into a claim it does not hold, and the two-tokens-named-ci flaw stops being reachable. What could break: an external MCP client that reports without a fence is refused on a leased row. The refusal text names the missing field, and the in-repo client is updated in the same series.

## Evaluation
Claim: correctness - every post-claim write is fenced to the claim generation that authorized it.
Before: 0 of 7 acceptance cases pass
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first against the existing CAS-faithful fake Prisma (followup-claims.test.ts pattern) and the handlers-write mock
Result: better
Gate: contract

## Summary
The ledger can show that an agent gave up on a row ('needs human'), and who holds it, but it offers no action on either fact. The shipped CLI flags every unattended run this way, the flag never clears, and the fix prompt still includes work another agent holds. Add the missing claim verbs (take over, send back, release) and let the prompt leave out held work.

## Description
The needs-human chip describes itself as the one state 'only a person can clear' (FollowupChips.tsx:18), but no code path clears it. The row stays in_progress with a null lease, so the lazy sweep treats it like a human claim and never releases it. Rescans carry the flag forward (scans-persist.ts:81). `npx ascent work run` reports needs_human for every id it claimed (ascent-work.mjs:178-193), so a team using the shipped client collects rows that only resolve or dismiss can move. Neither is the decision the person is actually making: 'I'll take this' or 'put it back for the next agent'.

A hand-off has the same gap: a person who handed off a batch and never pasted it cannot release it. And the prompt modal includes rows under another worker's live lease (FollowupsPromptModal.tsx:35-36), a merge conflict the loop lane already refuses (loop-lane.ts:1111). The ledger already has the data each decision needs (claimActor, claimExecutor, leaseUntil, needsHuman on every row, org-insights.ts:720-724).

This applies remediation-handoff / handoff-tenancy-and-idempotence (one CAS arbiter per write, whole-request refusal for a person's batch, foreign == unknown, a cap of 50, public org refused) to the human verbs.

## Flow
- `claimActionsModel.ts` (pure): `claimActionsFor(row, viewer, now)` and `promptPartition(rows, viewer, now)`. Authorization: take over = any member, on a needs-human row only; send back = a needs-human row or, for an admin, any claim; release = the holder's own human claim, or an admin.
- `followup-claims-human.ts`: `takeOverEscalations`, `sendBack` and `releaseHumanClaims`, each an org-scoped compare-and-set with one event per row and one audit row per batch (`followup.takeover` / `followup.release`).

## Expected impact
An escalation becomes a one-click decision instead of a permanent chip, a stalled hand-off can be returned to the queue, and a pasted prompt never sends a person into a row an agent is editing. Measured as needsHuman rows older than one scan (today they never fall) and as prompt batches containing a live foreign lease (target 0). What could break: an admin's send-back pulls work from a live agent, whose late report is then refused as not-held (with card A, refused as stale), which is the intended loud failure.
